analogy.p: Imagine three huge conveyor belts running between a boiler room (the equator) and a cold store (the poles). The first belt lifts hot air at the boiler room, carries it high up, drops it at 30 degrees and slides it back along the floor. The second and third belts are like gears meshed with it, one turning the opposite way, passing heat on to the cold store. Hot air rises where the belts lift (low pressure, wet) and cold air drops where they unload (high pressure, dry). The analogy breaks down because real air does not travel in tidy loops: the cells are only averages, with the jet streams, land and oceans constantly disturbing them.
analogy.t: A three-lane conveyor belt of heat

bullets: Know the **three cells in each hemisphere**: Hadley (0 to 30 degrees), Ferrel (30 to 60 degrees) and Polar (60 to 90 degrees).
Know the **pressure belts**: low at the equator (about 0 degrees), high at about 30 degrees, low at about 60 degrees, high at the poles (90 degrees).
Know the **surface winds**: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies, and which way each blows.
Be able to **explain why** air rises or sinks in each place, not only where it does.
Be able to annotate or complete a labelled diagram of the model, which is a very common exam task.
Be able to link the model to **climate and weather** (rainforests, deserts, UK depressions, tropical storm formation).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 (Paper 1, The challenge of natural hazards, weather hazards) requires **an understanding of the global atmospheric circulation model: pressure belts and surface winds**. In practice that means you must be able to describe and explain how the atmosphere moves air from the equator towards the poles, name the three cells, say where the **high and low pressure belts** are, and give the direction of the **surface winds** in each cell. The model is the foundation for the next two topics: tropical storms (which form in the trade wind belt) and UK weather (which is shaped by the westerlies and the polar front).

bullets: **Insolation** (incoming solar radiation) is highest at the equator and lowest at the poles.
At the equator the rays are concentrated on a small area; at the poles the same energy is spread over a much larger area.
Rays at high latitude travel through a longer path of atmosphere, so more is absorbed, scattered or reflected before reaching the ground.
Polar ice and snow have a high **albedo**, reflecting most of the energy that does arrive.
Without circulation, the equator would keep getting hotter and the poles colder; the global circulation moves heat from areas of surplus to areas of deficit.
The atmosphere does this by convection: warm air rises, cool air sinks, and winds move air between the two.
Ocean currents do part of the heat transfer too, but the spec point is about the atmosphere.
core.h: Why the atmosphere circulates: uneven heating
core.p: The whole system is driven by the fact that the Sun heats the Earth **unevenly**. At the equator the Sun is high in the sky, so its rays strike the surface almost vertically. The same amount of energy is concentrated onto a **small surface area** and passes through a **thin layer of atmosphere**, so less is absorbed or reflected on the way down. At the poles the Sun is low, so the same energy is spread over a **larger area** and passes through a **thicker layer of atmosphere**, losing more energy on the way. Ice and snow at the poles also reflect a lot of radiation (high albedo). The result is that the tropics receive more energy than they lose and the poles lose more than they receive, so the atmosphere (and the oceans) must transfer heat from the equator to the poles to balance the difference.

bullets: Low pressure (a **depression** or low) = rising air = cloud, rain and often wind.
High pressure (an **anticyclone** or high) = sinking air = clear skies, dry, settled weather.
Surface winds blow **from high to low pressure**.
Winds are named after the direction they blow **from**: a westerly wind blows from the west.
Rising warm air carries a lot of water vapour; as it rises it cools to its **dew point**, so vapour condenses and clouds form.
Sinking air warms as it is compressed, so any cloud evaporates; this is why deserts lie under high pressure.
core.h: Air pressure and wind: the basic rules
core.p: Before using the model you need three simple ideas. **Warm air is less dense, so it rises**; rising air leaves less air near the surface and so makes **low pressure**. **Cool air is denser, so it sinks**; sinking air piles up air near the surface and makes **high pressure**. **Wind is air moving from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure**, trying to even out the difference; the bigger the pressure difference, the stronger the wind. Rising air cools, so water vapour condenses into cloud and rain, whereas sinking air warms and dries, so skies are clear.

bullets: Air **rises at the equator** (low pressure, ITCZ), **flows poleward at height**, **sinks at 30 degrees** (high pressure) and **returns along the surface to the equator**.
The surface return flow is the **trade winds**: from the north-east in the northern hemisphere and from the south-east in the southern hemisphere.
The trade winds converge at the ITCZ, which is why it is called the convergence zone.
The rising branch gives the **tropical rainforest** climate: hot, wet all year with daily convectional rain.
The sinking branch gives the world's **hot deserts** (for example the Sahara and Arabian deserts, the Australian deserts and the Kalahari).
The ITCZ moves a little north and south with the overhead Sun through the year, which causes wet and dry seasons in many tropical areas.
Tropical storms form over warm oceans in the trade wind belt, so the Hadley cell is directly relevant to the next topic.
core.p: The Hadley cell is the largest and strongest cell and is the one most likely to be tested. At the **equator** intense heating makes air **rise**, creating a belt of **low pressure** called the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**. As the air rises it cools and condenses, giving heavy rain and thunderstorms. At height the air cannot rise forever and spreads out **towards the poles**. By about **30 degrees north and south** it has cooled and become dense, so it **sinks**, forming a belt of **high pressure** with dry, clear conditions. When it reaches the ground, some air flows back towards the equator along the surface as the **trade winds**, completing the loop.

bullets: Air **sinks at the poles** (high pressure), **flows along the surface towards 60 degrees**, **rises at 60 degrees** (low pressure) and **returns at height to the poles**.
The surface winds are the **polar easterlies**: cold winds blowing from the north-east in the northern hemisphere and the south-east in the southern hemisphere.
Because the air is sinking and very cold, it holds little moisture, so polar regions are dry (cold deserts) despite all the ice.
The boundary where cold polar air meets warm air from the south is the **polar front**, near 60 degrees; fronts and depressions form along it.
The Polar cell is the weakest of the three cells because the temperature difference driving it is smaller and the area is smaller.
core.p: At the poles the surface is very cold, so the air above it is cold and dense and **sinks**, creating permanent **high pressure** at about **90 degrees north and south**. This cold air flows out along the surface towards lower latitudes. By about **60 degrees** it meets warmer air from the Ferrel cell. Because the cold air is denser, the warmer air is forced up over the top of it and **rises**, creating a belt of **low pressure** at about 60 degrees. Some of that air returns at height towards the poles, completing the Polar cell.

bullets: Surface flow in the Ferrel cell is **poleward**, from high pressure at 30 degrees to low pressure at 60 degrees.
The surface winds are the **westerlies** (south-westerlies in the northern hemisphere, north-westerlies in the southern hemisphere).
Warm, moist air from the south-west meets cold air from the north at the **polar front**, making **depressions**.
The UK is at about 50 to 60 degrees north, in the westerly belt near the polar front, so it has **frequent low pressure systems** and variable weather.
The Ferrel cell is an **indirect cell**: it is moved by the friction and flow of the Hadley and Polar cells either side.
In the exam, you can say the Ferrel cell has **rising air at 60 degrees** and **sinking air at 30 degrees**.
core.p: The Ferrel cell sits between the Hadley and Polar cells and works rather like a gear wheel turned by its two neighbours instead of being driven directly by heating. At the surface air flows **from the 30 degree high pressure towards the 60 degree low pressure**, that is, **poleward**. At 60 degrees it **rises** (the same rising air that is part of the Polar cell's circuit) and returns at height towards 30 degrees, where it **sinks**. The warm air moving poleward at the surface meets cold polar air at the polar front and is forced up over it, which creates the low pressure systems that bring the UK its changeable, wet weather.

bullets: **0 degrees (equator): LOW** pressure, air rising, ITCZ, rainforests.
**30 degrees N and S: HIGH** pressure, air sinking, dry, hot deserts.
**60 degrees N and S: LOW** pressure, air rising, polar front, depressions (UK weather).
**90 degrees (poles): HIGH** pressure, cold air sinking, cold deserts.
Where cells meet at the surface and air **converges** (equator, 60 degrees), it has nowhere to go but up, so it rises.
Where air **diverges** at the surface (30 degrees, poles), it flows away and is replaced by sinking air from above.
Remember: **rising air = low pressure = wet; sinking air = high pressure = dry**.
core.p: Putting the three cells together gives alternating belts of low and high pressure from the equator to the pole. Air **rises** where surface winds from two cells meet and converge (at the equator and at 60 degrees) and **sinks** where the upper-level flows from two cells meet (at 30 degrees and at the poles). Learn the pattern as **Low, High, Low, High** starting at the equator: 0 degrees low, 30 degrees high, 60 degrees low, 90 degrees high. The pattern is **mirrored in the southern hemisphere**.

bullets: **Trade winds (0 to 30 degrees):** blow towards the equator, deflected to become north-easterlies in the north and south-easterlies in the south.
**Westerlies (30 to 60 degrees):** blow towards the poles, deflected to become south-westerlies in the north and north-westerlies in the south.
**Polar easterlies (60 to 90 degrees):** blow towards lower latitudes, becoming north-easterlies in the north and south-easterlies in the south.
The Coriolis effect is **zero at the equator** and strongest at the poles; this is why tropical storms cannot form within about 5 degrees of the equator.
In the northern hemisphere low pressure systems spin **anticlockwise** and highs spin clockwise; it is reversed in the southern hemisphere.
Winds are named by where they come **from**, so the trade winds in the northern hemisphere are called the **north-east trades**.
core.h: Surface winds and the Coriolis effect
core.p: If the Earth did not spin, surface winds would blow straight north or south along the pressure gradient. Because the Earth **rotates**, moving air is **deflected**: to the **right in the northern hemisphere** and to the **left in the southern hemisphere**. This is the **Coriolis effect**. It turns the north-to-south flow of the trade winds into a flow from the north-east, turns the south-to-north flow in the Ferrel cell into a flow from the south-west, and turns the polar flow into a flow from the north-east. In the southern hemisphere the deflection is the other way, giving south-east trade winds, north-westerlies and south-easterly polar winds.

bullets: **Equator:** rising air, heavy daily rain, tropical rainforest (Amazon, Congo, South East Asia).
**About 30 degrees:** sinking air, clear skies, extreme day temperatures, hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Atacama, Australian).
**About 50 to 60 degrees:** rising air at the polar front, frequent depressions, mild wet climates (UK, Western Europe).
**Poles:** sinking cold air, very low precipitation, polar deserts (Antarctica is the driest continent).
The ITCZ shifts north in northern summer and south in southern summer, producing **seasonal rainfall** (monsoons, wet and dry seasons).
The model is an **average, simplified** picture; real weather varies because of land, mountains, ocean currents and the shifting seasons.
core.h: How the model explains world climates
core.p: The global circulation explains why the same latitudes have similar climates all over the world. Where air is **rising** at low pressure (equator, 60 degrees) there is cloud and rain; where air is **sinking** at high pressure (30 degrees and the poles) there is little cloud and little rain. This is why the biggest hot deserts lie close to 30 degrees north and south and the great rainforests lie on or near the equator. The model also shows why the UK, where tropical and polar air meet, has changeable weather rather than a stable climate.

bullets: Storms form where the trade winds converge near the low-pressure ITCZ over oceans warmer than 27 degrees Celsius.
The trade winds push storms **east to west** (towards the Caribbean, the Philippines, Queensland, Madagascar).
At about 30 degrees the storm meets the westerlies and curves **poleward and eastward**, where it loses strength over cold water.
Seasonal movement of the ITCZ shifts the main storm season: late summer and autumn in each hemisphere.
Remember the link for the 6 mark question: **global circulation to warm ocean to storm formation to track**.
core.p: Tropical storms form in the **Hadley cell**, between about 5 and 30 degrees north and south, where the trade winds blow across warm oceans. Warm, moist air is already rising there and the Coriolis effect is just strong enough to make the rising air spin. The trade winds also **steer** tropical storms westwards across the ocean; when a storm reaches about 25 to 30 degrees it meets the **westerlies**, which turn it towards the east and the poles. So the pressure belts and winds explain both **where storms form** and **which way they travel**.

bullets: The prevailing wind in the UK is **south-westerly**, bringing warm, moist air from the Atlantic.
Depressions form along the **polar front** and are steered east by the westerlies over the UK.
Extreme UK weather (storms, heavy rain, floods) is often linked to **strong low pressure systems** moving in off the Atlantic.
Cold, dry weather in winter can come when the wind shifts to a **polar or easterly** direction.
This is covered in more detail under UK extreme weather.
core.p: The UK lies in the Ferrel cell near the polar front at about 50 to 60 degrees north. Warm, moist **south-westerly** air from the Atlantic meets cold **polar** air, and the warm air is forced up, creating **depressions** (areas of low pressure) that travel eastwards on the westerlies. Depressions bring cloud, rain and wind. Between them, areas of high pressure (anticyclones) bring settled, dry weather. This is why the UK has such changeable weather and, with the Atlantic nearby, a mostly mild, wet climate.

bullets: **Strengths:** explains the main pressure belts and winds; explains why deserts and rainforests lie where they do; helps predict storm tracks.
**Limits:** averages only; ignores continents, mountains and seasons; the Ferrel cell is a mathematical idea more than a real simple loop.
Land heats and cools faster than sea, so **monsoons** reverse the wind pattern seasonally, which the basic model does not show.
Real day-to-day weather is controlled by moving pressure systems and fronts rather than a steady pattern.
In an evaluation question, give **one strength and one limitation** and reach a judgement.
core.h: Higher-level evaluation: strengths and limits of the model
core.p: The three-cell model is a **simplification**. It describes average conditions over a year and over all longitudes, and it ignores land, mountains and ocean currents. Real circulation is complicated by the **jet streams** (fast, high-altitude winds near the cell boundaries), by monsoons, and by land and sea heating differently. Still, it explains the major climate zones well and gives a firm basis for understanding weather hazards.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark):** give one fact only, for example 'The trade winds blow from the north-east' or 'The pressure at 30 degrees is high'.
**Describe (2 to 3 marks):** make 2 or 3 separate points. For a labelled diagram of the model, describe the direction of air movement and the pressure at each latitude.
**Explain (3 to 4 marks):** each mark is a 'because' link. Model chain: Intense heating at the equator, so air rises, creating low pressure; the rising air cools and condenses, so heavy rain.
**Annotate a diagram:** usually label the cells, add arrows for rising and sinking air, mark high and low pressure, and add surface wind names. Copy the arrow directions carefully.
**Link to climate:** if asked why deserts are at 30 degrees, say 'air sinks, warms, so clouds evaporate and little rainfall'.
**Compare (4 marks):** use comparative words (whereas, but, while) and give both sides, for example Hadley versus Polar cell.
**Link to tropical storms (6 marks):** write about the Hadley cell, trade winds, ITCZ, warm ocean (27 degrees Celsius), Coriolis effect and then the track; link each idea with 'so' or 'therefore'.
**Always use the exact terms:** pressure belts, rising air, sinking air, trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies, ITCZ, Coriolis effect.
**Tip:** if you forget the pattern, remember 'Low, High, Low, High' from the equator, and that wind goes from high to low.
**Tip:** check your wind directions by deflection: right in the northern hemisphere, left in the southern hemisphere.

mistakes.r: Winds blow from high pressure to low pressure.
mistakes.w: Winds blow from low pressure to high pressure.

mistakes.r: A westerly wind blows from the west (towards the east).
mistakes.w: A westerly wind blows towards the west.

mistakes.r: There is high pressure at 30 degrees because air is sinking there.
mistakes.w: There is low pressure at 30 degrees because it is hot.

mistakes.r: Air rises at the equator because intense heating makes it warm, less dense and buoyant.
mistakes.w: Air rises at the equator because it is windy.

mistakes.r: Pressure differences cause wind; the Coriolis effect only deflects it (right in the north, left in the south).
The big hot deserts are dry mainly because they lie under the 30 degree high pressure belt, where air sinks, warms and clouds cannot form.
mistakes.w: Deserts are dry because they are far from the sea.

mistakes.r: In the Ferrel cell, air sinks at 30 degrees and rises at 60 degrees.
mistakes.w: The Ferrel cell has rising air at 30 degrees.

mistakes.r: The trade winds blow towards the equator, from the north-east in the north and the south-east in the south.
mistakes.w: The trade winds blow away from the equator.

mistakes.r: Polar regions are dry (cold deserts) because cold air sinks and holds little moisture.
mistakes.w: Polar regions are wet because there is so much ice.

summary: You need to understand the global atmospheric circulation model: three cells in each hemisphere (Hadley, Ferrel, Polar), the alternating belts of low and high pressure at 0, 30, 60 and 90 degrees, and the surface winds (trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies). It matters because it explains where tropical storms form and travel, why deserts and rainforests lie where they do, and why the UK has changeable weather, so it is the foundation for the whole weather hazards topic.

terms.d: The large-scale movement of air around the Earth that transfers heat from the equator to the poles.
The circulation cell between 0 and 30 degrees latitude: air rises at the equator, flows poleward at height, sinks at about 30 degrees and returns along the surface as trade winds.
The middle cell between 30 and 60 degrees: air sinks at 30 degrees, flows poleward at the surface as westerlies and rises at 60 degrees.
The cell between 60 and 90 degrees: cold air sinks at the pole, flows along the surface as polar easterlies and rises at 60 degrees.
Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone: the belt of low pressure at the equator where the trade winds meet and air rises, giving heavy rain.
A band of persistently high or low atmospheric pressure at a particular latitude.
Steady surface winds blowing towards the equator within the Hadley cell, from the north-east in the north and the south-east in the south.
Prevailing surface winds between 30 and 60 degrees, blowing from the south-west in the northern hemisphere and the north-west in the southern.
Cold surface winds blowing from the poles towards 60 degrees, from the north-east in the north and south-east in the south.
The deflection of moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere, caused by the Earth's rotation.
An area where air is rising; associated with cloud, rain and wind.
An area where air is sinking; associated with clear skies and dry, settled weather.
The boundary near 60 degrees where warm air from the Ferrel cell meets cold air from the Polar cell and is forced to rise, forming depressions.
Incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth's surface.
The proportion of incoming radiation reflected by a surface; ice and snow have a high albedo.
Air flowing together at the surface, forcing it to rise.
A low pressure weather system with rising air, bringing cloud, rain and wind.
A high pressure weather system with sinking air, bringing settled, dry weather.

worked.ans: The Sun's rays strike the equator almost vertically, so the surface is heated intensely. This warms the air above it, making it less dense, so it rises. Rising air leaves less air at the surface, creating a belt of low pressure (the ITCZ), and as it rises it cools and condenses, forming clouds and heavy rain.
worked.q: Explain why there is low pressure at the equator. (3 marks)
steps: Link to air movement: warm air is less dense and rises.
Link to pressure: rising air leaves less air at the surface, so pressure is low.
Add a consequence to strengthen: cooling, condensation, heavy rain.

worked.ans: Between 0 and 30 degrees north the trade winds blow towards the equator from the north-east. Between 30 and 60 degrees the westerlies blow towards the poles from the south-west. Between 60 and 90 degrees the polar easterlies blow from the north-east. All winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected to the right by the Coriolis effect.
worked.q: Describe the pattern of surface winds in the northern hemisphere in the global atmospheric circulation model. (4 marks)
steps: Give the trade winds with direction and latitudes.
Give the westerlies with direction and latitudes.
Give the polar easterlies with direction and latitudes.
Link at least one to pressure or the Coriolis effect.

worked.ans: In the Hadley cell, air that rose at the equator flows towards the poles at height and cools. By about 30 degrees it is dense and sinks, creating a belt of high pressure. As the air sinks it warms and can hold more water vapour, so clouds evaporate and skies are clear. Little rain falls and there are high daytime temperatures, so hot deserts form.
worked.q: Using the global atmospheric circulation model, explain why many hot deserts are found near 30 degrees north and south. (4 marks)
steps: State the circulation: Hadley cell air flows poleward at height.
Explain cooling and sinking at 30 degrees.
Explain high pressure and warming of descending air.
Link to lack of cloud and rain.
